A stationary baseline downlink experiment measures delivered application throughput, mean end-to-end application delay, and undelivered packets. Compare per-UE throughput and delay ranges to identify uneven delivery. Undelivered packets can include packets still in flight at simulation stop time and must not automatically be interpreted as radio packet loss. Baseline measurements alone do not establish handover failures, interference, or energy savings. Compare measured performance against explicit operator targets; without targets, do not claim SLA compliance or infer a fault.

Energy optimization in RAN clusters should preserve QoS while reducing transmit power or placing low-load sectors into sleep states. Validate the change with before/after KPIs: throughput, latency, packet loss, SINR, and handover success. Avoid deep sleep on sectors with active mobility hotspots or poor neighbor coverage.

ETSI ETSI TS 103 982 V8.0.0 (2024 -01) 24 6.6 O-RAN Security Architecture 6.6.1 Introduction to O-RAN Security Architecture The goal of the O-RAN ALLIANCE is to achieve a secure, open, and interoperable RAN. Building upon security advancements from the 3GPP and IETF standards development organizations, the O-RAN ALLIANCE is specifying an O-RAN security architecture that enables 5G CSP (Communi cation Service Providers) to deploy and operate O-RAN with the same level of confidence as a 3GPP-specified RAN. The O-RAN ALLIANCE is strengthening O-RAN's security posture by mitigating risk across its attack surface while pursuing the goals of a ZTA (Zero-Trust Architecture). O-RAN activities are guided by the following objectives [i.4]: • Leading the industry towards open, interoperable interfaces, RAN virtualization, and big data and AI enabled RAN intelligence. • Maximizing the use of common-off-the-shelf hardware and merchant silicon and minimizing proprietary hardware. • Specifying APIs and interfaces, driving standards to adopt them as appropriate, and exploring open source where appropriate. • The O-RAN Architecture identifies the key functions and interfaces adopted in O-RAN.

High handover failure rate is commonly associated with weak coverage overlap, late A3 event triggering, excessive X2 latency, or high UE mobility. Recommended checks: verify neighbor relation tables, reduce A3 offset if triggers are late, lower time-to-trigger for high-speed corridors, inspect X2/backhaul delay, and compare SINR near cell borders.

Throughput degradation with low SINR and high PRB utilization suggests interference or hotspot overload. Recommended checks: inspect co-channel interference, scheduler pressure, antenna tilt, neighboring cell load, and handover imbalance. Remediation can include load balancing, power tuning, antenna optimization, and slice-specific policy adjustment.

TelcoMind mobility handover experiments use linear UE movement, dynamic cell association, enabled NR handovers, and X2 links between all seven base stations. Serving-cell vectors record simulator node IDs. Exclude initial association and count subsequent ID changes as serving-cell transitions; report transitions to node ID zero separately as detachments. A transition count is not a handover attempt denominator or a standardized success rate. Correlate transition times with measured downlink throughput and delay, but do not infer a handover failure solely from an undelivered packet. No controlled handover fault is injected.

TelcoMind resource comparison experiments execute two fresh stationary downlink runs with identical UE count, seed, duration, packet size, and send interval. Only the configured number of resource bands differs. Compare candidate minus reference throughput, mean delay, and undelivered percentage points. Equal performance can mean the tested load did not expose a resource constraint; do not invent an improvement. Resource band changes are not network slicing or an automated remediation.

TelcoMind traffic burst experiments increase downlink UDP offered traffic during a bounded middle window while keeping stationary UEs and resource bands unchanged. Compare measured throughput and mean delay before, during, and after the burst. Phase throughput uses each observation window, including drain time in the final window. Increased offered traffic is not proof of congestion: establish whether delivery or delay deteriorated using measured results and explicit targets. This experiment does not inject radio interference.

## energy_optimization Operator intent examples: - Reduce energy usage while preserving service quality. - Evaluate whether cells, carriers, or features can enter energy-saving modes during low demand. - Confirm that energy optimization does not degrade coverage, latency, or mobility. Likely simulation KPIs: - Energy consumption per cell, carrier, or site. - Cell load, PRB utilization, and traffic demand. - UE throughput and latency before and after optimization. - Coverage indicators such as RSRP, RSRQ, and SINR. - Handover success rate after energy-saving actions. RAG evidence expected: - Energy-saving runbooks and operator policy notes. - Standards or architecture references for RAN energy efficiency, capacity management, sleep modes, and service continuity in general terms. - Baseline scenario evidence showing normal traffic and quality before optimization. Remediation and diagnostic relevance: - Supports safe recommendations such as staged energy-saving activation, rollback conditions, and KPI guardrails. - Helps identify when poor quality is caused by overly aggressive energy saving. - Links energy actions to customer-impact checks before automation.

## handover_failure Operator intent examples: - Diagnose why UEs drop sessions or lose throughput during mobility. - Identify whether failures are linked to radio conditions, neighbor configuration, load, or timing. - Recommend corrective actions that improve handover reliability without causing unnecessary handovers. Likely simulation KPIs: - Handover success rate and failure rate. - Radio link failure count. - Drop call or session interruption rate. - RSRP, RSRQ, and SINR around serving and target cells. - Time-to-trigger, hysteresis behavior, and neighbor relation indicators when available. RAG evidence expected: - Mobility and handover troubleshooting runbooks. - Standards or technical references describing measurement reporting, handover decision logic, and neighbor cell management in general terms. - Prior incident notes for mobility failures, coverage gaps, ping-pong handovers, or overloaded target cells. Remediation and diagnostic relevance: - Supports recommendations such as checking neighbor relations, tuning mobility parameters, balancing target cell load, or investigating coverage holes. - Helps separate radio-quality failures from policy or configuration issues. - Provides evidence for whether intervention should be local to a cell pair or broader across a mobility region.

## interference_hotspot Operator intent examples: - Detect localized radio interference affecting user experience. - Identify whether degraded SINR is caused by load, coverage, neighboring cells, or external interference. - Recommend diagnostics and mitigation steps for affected cells or sectors. Likely simulation KPIs: - SINR, RSRP, and RSRQ distribution. - UE throughput degradation by location or cell. - Packet loss, latency, and retransmission indicators when available. - Cell edge performance. - PRB utilization and neighboring-cell activity. RAG evidence expected: - Radio interference troubleshooting runbooks. - Standards or technical references describing radio measurements, interference coordination, and radio resource management in general terms. - Historical notes for hotspot patterns, sector-specific degradation, or recurring interference windows. Remediation and diagnostic relevance: - Supports recommendations such as checking neighboring-cell configuration, validating power settings, reviewing spectrum conditions, and correlating degraded SINR with traffic load. - Helps separate true interference from ordinary congestion or weak coverage. - Provides evidence for whether mitigation should target radio parameters, physical inspection, or capacity planning.
